findings.source_passage: "Aye, lad, thou shalt sit here in my own screwed chair; another screw to it, thou must be."
findings.why_it_matters: The 'screwed chair' line establishes the chair as a charged object that recurs in Pip's subsequent soliloquy; without it, Pip's later claim 'this screwed chair was mine' loses its dramatic anchor and the interpretive symmetry collapses.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the closing lines of Ahab's first speech verbatim: 'Aye, lad, thou shalt sit here in my own screwed chair; another screw to it, thou must be.'

findings.source_passage: "Oh! spite of million villains, this makes me a bigot in the fadeless fidelity of man!—and a black! and crazy!—but methinks like-cures-like applies to him too; he grows so sane again."
findings.source_locator: Ahab's aside between Pip's first and second speeches
findings.why_it_matters: This is an interpretively critical passage — Ahab's acknowledgment of Pip's humanizing power on him ('fadeless fidelity of man'), his self-implication, and his recognition of Pip's paradoxical sanity. Critics return to it repeatedly; its excision removes a defining beat of the Ahab-Pip relationship.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore this aside in full; it cannot be summarized without loss of its rhetorical and thematic weight.

findings.source_passage: "They tell me, sir, that Stubb did once desert poor little Pip, whose drowned bones now show white, for all the blackness of his living skin. But I will never desert ye, sir, as Stubb did him."
findings.why_it_matters: This speech is interpretively essential: Pip's self-referential third-person dissociation ('poor little Pip, whose drowned bones now show white') is a key marker of his psychological fracture and carries major critical weight. Its removal erases the motif of self-estrangement.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore Pip's second speech verbatim; the self-referential third-person is not compressible without destroying the passage's meaning.

findings.source_passage: "And now I quit thee. Thy hand!—Met! True art thou, lad, as the circumference to its centre."
findings.why_it_matters: The draft omits 'And now I quit thee' and begins mid-sentence, but more critically omits the stage direction '(_Ahab goes; Pip steps one step forward._)' which is essential framing for what follows.
findings.suggested_fix: Retain the full closing of Ahab's speech and the stage direction marking Ahab's departure and Pip's single step forward.

findings.source_passage: "Here he this instant stood; I stand in his air,—but I'm alone. Now were even poor Pip here I could endure it, but he's missing. Pip! Pip! Ding, dong, ding!"
findings.source_locator: Pip's soliloquy after Ahab's departure, opening lines
findings.why_it_matters: Pip's post-departure soliloquy is one of the most distinctive passages in the novel — fragmented, dissociative, moving from self-estrangement to mock-grandiosity to pathos. The draft replaces the entire soliloquy with a single summary sentence, erasing one of Melville's most remarkable examples of dramatic ventriloquism.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore Pip's soliloquy in full or in very close paraphrase; at minimum the opening dissociation ('I stand in his air—but I'm alone'), the mock-admiral scene, and the closing 'Hist! above there, I hear ivory—Oh, master! master!' must be preserved.

findings.source_passage: "epaulets! epaulets! the epaulets all come crowding! Pass round the decanters; glad to see ye; fill up, monsieurs! What an odd feeling, now, when a black boy's host to white men with gold lace upon their coats!"
findings.why_it_matters: The mock-admiral scene with its racial inversion ('a black boy's host to white men') is critically celebrated for its tragicomic irony and its commentary on race and power; its complete absence is a major interpretive and voice loss.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore this passage; it is not a dispensable digression but the thematic and tonal heart of the chapter's second half.

findings.source_passage: "But here I'll stay, though this stern strikes rocks; and they bulge through; and oysters come to join me."
findings.why_it_matters: The closing image — the ship striking rocks, hull breached, oysters joining Pip at the bottom — is one of Melville's strangest and most haunting closures, and the chapter's final image; its loss removes the chapter's ending entirely.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore as the chapter's closing line verbatim.

summary: The draft catastrophically excises Pip's entire post-departure soliloquy — the interpretively and stylistically richest passage in the chapter — along with Ahab's aside on 'fadeless fidelity,' Pip's self-estranging third-person speech, and the screwed-chair lines, constituting total voice erasure of the chapter's second half and loss of multiple high-priority signatures.
